title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
challenge_note: Cool flame dynamics of droplets under external perturbation.
objective: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.
hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
approach:
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.
research_impacts:
Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

findings.conditions_text: n-dodecane droplets burning in air; (do = 4.00 mm)
findings.statement: For n-dodecane droplets burning in air, the cool-flame extinction diameter decreases as pressure increases and is absent at 3 atm, where the droplet burns to completion following warm-flame combustion.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction assessments for pressurized spacecraft environments should account for pressure-dependent cool-flame behavior and the possibility of continued warm-flame combustion.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control and fire-risk assessments should account for pressure effects on cool-flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: Both hot and cool flame extinction diameter has a non-linear dependence on pressure. de,CF decreases as pressure is increased, and is absent at 3 atm as the droplet burns to completion following a “Warm” flame combustion

findings.conditions_text: three fuels
findings.quantity: cool-flame extinction properties and hot-flame extinction behavior
findings.statement: For the three n-alkane fuels, larger molecules exhibited more robust, higher-temperature cool flames and smaller extinction diameters; hot-flame extinction behavior was predicted to be similar across the fuels.
findings.safety_implication: Cool-flame extinction expectations should be fuel-specific; similarity in hot-flame behavior does not establish similar cool-flame behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Fuel-specific extinction assessments should include cool-flame behavior rather than infer it from hot-flame results.
findings.source_quote: Hot flame characteristics of all three fuels indicate that predicted extinction phenomena are all very similar. Cool flame extinction properties are significantly affected by the n-alkane molecular weight, and the chain length of the n-alkane has significant effect on the cool flame reactivity - larger n-alkane exhibited more robust cool flame (i.e., higher temperature) and hence smaller extinction diameters.

findings.conditions_text: ambient pressures above one atmosphere
findings.statement: For n-dodecane droplet combustion, single two-stage hot-cool flame transitions changed to multi-cycle combustion above one atmosphere and eventually to a hot-to-warm flame transition as ambient pressure increased.
findings.safety_implication: Combustion behavior established at one pressure may not predict droplet flame transitions at higher operating pressures.
findings.equipment_implication: Pressure-dependent combustion modes should be considered when assessing spacecraft atmosphere operating conditions.
findings.source_quote: n-Dodecane droplet combustion reveal a strong dependence of observations on ambient pressure. Single, two-stage hot-cool flame combustion transitions to a multi-cycle combustion behavior at ambient pressures above one atmosphere, and eventually into a hot - “Warm” flame transition.

findings.conditions_text: xenon-rich environment
findings.quantity: burning time and flame temperature compared with other diluents/extinguishers
findings.statement: In microgravity methanol combustion, xenon-rich environments produced longer burning times and higher flame temperatures than other tested diluents or extinguishers, and supported hot flames at lower oxygen content.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon may be a poor choice for spacecraft fire suppression because it can prolong burning and sustain hot flames at lower oxygen levels.
findings.equipment_implication: The reported combustion behavior argues against adopting xenon as a next-generation microgravity fire suppressant.
findings.source_quote: The comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burning time and higher flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguishers and can support hot flame with much lesser oxygen content than its counterparts.

findings.conditions_text: xenon (Xe) enriched environments
findings.statement: Numerical simulations predict that methanol droplets burning in xenon-enriched environments have a reduced burning rate, larger extinction diameter, and prolonged burning time compared with other ambient conditions studied.
findings.safety_implication: The prolonged burning time and larger extinction diameter mean xenon enrichment may not reliably shorten the hazard period or promote extinction in reduced-gravity fire scenarios.
findings.equipment_implication: Xenon should not be assumed to be an effective fire-suppression diluent for reduced-gravity applications.
findings.source_quote: It is found that xenon augmented ambient results in reduced burning rate, larger extinction diameter and counter-intuitively, prolonged burning time.

findings.conditions_text: xenon, argon, carbon dioxide or helium as diluents
findings.statement: Numerical analyses find that the limiting oxygen index for methanol combustion in xenon is significantly lower than in argon, carbon dioxide, or helium, with xenon's lower thermal diffusivity identified as the principal cause.
findings.safety_implication: An atmosphere containing xenon may support methanol combustion at lower oxygen levels than these alternative diluents, so oxygen thresholds should not be transferred across diluent choices.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should account for the diluent because xenon has a lower predicted limiting oxygen index than argon, carbon dioxide, or helium.
findings.source_quote: The limiting oxygen index (LOI) for xenon is found be significantly lower than argon, carbon dioxide or helium. The numerical analyses also indicate that the lower thermal diffusivity of xenon is the principal factor responsible for the remarkably lower LOI.

findings.conditions_text: xenon as a diluent in reduced gravity applications
findings.statement: The authors conclude that xenon is unsuitable as a fire-suppression diluent for reduced-gravity applications because its associated elevated peak gas temperature, exceptionally slow diffusive heat loss, and lower limiting oxygen index detract from its suppression utility.
findings.equipment_implication: The authors advise against relying on xenon as a suppressive diluent in reduced-gravity fire-safety applications.
findings.source_quote: It is concluded that the combined observation of elevated peak gas temperature, exceptionally slow diffusive heat loss and the lower LOI value associated with xenon as a diluent all detract from its utility for suppressing fire concerns in reduced gravity applications.

findings.quantity: quasi-steady combustion behavior with diluent gas
findings.statement: For methanol droplets in the predicted cases, higher xenon displacement promoted rather than degraded quasi-steady combustion at low oxygen concentration, unlike helium and carbon dioxide dilution.
findings.safety_implication: Low oxygen concentration alone may not predict whether a droplet flame persists; the identity of the diluent can change the combustion response.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control analyses should treat xenon, helium, and carbon dioxide as distinct diluents rather than interchangeable oxygen-displacement agents.
findings.source_quote: Unlike the results for other diluents (helium, carbon dioxide), at increased loading condition (i.e. low oxygen concentration), higher xenon displacements promote rather than degrade quasi-steady combustion [4].

findings.conditions_text: 21% O2/79% Xe composition during the quasi-steady burn period; xenon mole fraction raised to 93% from 79% (Do = 2.0 mm)
findings.statement: For predicted microgravity combustion of methanol droplets, flame stand-off ratio depended weakly on initial droplet size and strongly on ambient gas composition; at 2.0 mm, increasing xenon from 79% to 93% raised FSR from about 5.0 to about 6.4.
findings.source_quote: For 21% O2/79% Xe composition, the FSR during the quasi-steady burn period was found to be ~ 5.0 for Do = 2.0 mm which then increased to ~5.5 for Do = 1.0 mm. However, when xenon mole fraction is raised to 93% from 79% (Do = 2.0 mm), the FSR escalates to ~ 6.4.

findings.equipment_implication: Oxygen-control criteria should account for the larger-droplet LOI reported in these simulations.
findings.source_quote: The LOI for Do values of 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm and 2.0 mm were found to be ~ 4%, 5%, and 6%, respectively.

findings.statement: The document reports that the xenon limiting oxygen index for a 1.5 mm methanol droplet at 1 atm was lower by a factor of 2.2 than the nitrogen value of 11% cited for the similar ambient condition.
findings.safety_implication: Do not transfer oxygen-limit criteria between diluents without accounting for the diluent-specific difference reported here.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should be established for the intended diluent rather than inferred from nitrogen data.
findings.source_quote: In contrast to the LOI results found for nitrogen (e.g., 11% for Do = 1.5 mm at 1 atm [4]), the LOI for xenon under the similar ambient condition is reduced by a factor of 2.2.

findings.statement: For methanol droplets with an initial diameter of 1.5 mm in microgravity, xenon had a lower limiting oxygen index (5%) than argon (8%), helium (21%), and carbon dioxide (21%), and its longer burn times indicate that xenon is a poor fire-suppressant diluent under these conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon dilution should not be relied on to suppress methanol droplet flames in microgravity, because flames can persist at substantially reduced oxygen concentrations.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression and atmosphere-control strategies should not treat xenon as an effective diluent for methanol droplet fires under these conditions.
findings.source_quote: For instance, LOI for Do =1.5 mm was found to be 5%, 8%, 21% and 21% for xenon, argon, helium and carbon dioxide respectively. The combination of a very low LOI and longer burn times points to xenon being a poor choice as a ‘fire suppressant’ diluent under microgravity conditions.

findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control assessments should account for the coupled changes in burning rate and extinction diameter as xenon content changes.
findings.source_quote: The droplet regression rate decreases with increasing xenon content (i.e. decreasing O2) for a fixed droplet diameter contributing reductions in burning rate and earlier flame extinction at larger extinction diameters.

findings.equipment_implication: Xenon-based atmosphere control or suppression strategies should not be selected as a fire-safety improvement on the basis of these results.

findings.quantity: combustion completion and soot shell formation

findings.safety_implication: The observed resistance to extinction suggests that small n-butanol droplets could remain burning rather than self-extinguish in comparable environments.
findings.source_quote: The experiments show no presence of a soot shell during the combustion process and droplets are observed to burn to completion unlike other smaller C1–C3 alcohols.

findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control and suppression strategies should not assume that reducing oxygen below ordinary ambient levels will extinguish n-butanol droplet flames.
findings.source_quote: The numerical analysis predicts that for sub-millimeter sized n-Butanol droplets, the limiting oxygen index is as low as 10% suggesting that flame extinction for n-Butanol is unlikely in practical applications.

findings.conditions_text: standard atmosphere conditions; isolated droplets with diameters ranged from 0.52 mm to 0.56 mm
findings.quantity: burning rate and flame stand-off ratio
findings.statement: For isolated butanol-isomer droplets under standard-atmosphere conditions, measured iso- and sec-butanol burning rates were very close to n-butanol's, while flame structure differed; n-butanol had smaller flame stand-off ratios than the isomers, and tert-butanol had the largest.
findings.safety_implication: Similar burning rates across these isomers do not imply identical flame geometry, so hazard assessments should account for the fuel isomer as well as burning rate.
findings.equipment_implication: Material and fuel hazard evaluations should distinguish butanol isomers because their flame structures and stand-off ratios differ.
findings.source_quote: The experimental data showed that the burning rates of iso- and sec-butanol are very close to that of n-butanol, differing only in flame structure. The flame stand-off ratios (FSR) for n-butanol flames are smaller than those for the isomers, while tert-butanol flames exhibited the largest FSR.
findings.earth_application: The measured combustion behavior can inform hazard assessment of butanol-isomer fuels used in ground transportation.

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter droplets; FSR evolution during burning
findings.quantity: agreement of kinetic-model FSR predictions with experiments
findings.statement: For sec-, iso-, and tert-butanol droplet combustion, the MIT kinetic model reproduced FSR evolution, particularly with the maximum-heat-release-rate marker, while the LLNL model consistently overpredicted FSR from the start of burning.
findings.source_quote: For sec-, iso- and tert-butanol isomers, the MIT model correctly simulated the FSR evolution, especially with HRRmax approach. Although the model’s prediction capability is laudable for sec- and iso-butanol, disagreement for tert-butanol at the latter part of the burn time is noticeable. Surprisingly, for all the isomers reported here, LLNL model consistently over-predicts the FSR evolution from initial burn time with similar FSR trend throughout its burning period and ultimately exhibiting almost the same extinction/flame-out temporal location (t/( Do)2 ∼1.20-1.25 s/mm2).

findings.conditions_text: computationally investigated for atmospheric and higher operating pressure (25 atm) conditions with varying levels of ozone (O3) mole fractions in the surroundings
findings.quantity: cool-flame burning mode and transition to hot flames
findings.statement: For computationally modeled sub-millimeter n-heptane and n-decane droplets, cool-flame regime and transition behavior depended on ozone loading, pressure, diluent, initiation-source strength, and fuel vapor pressure; sustained cool burning without transition to a hot flame was possible over some combinations of ozone concentration, pressure, and droplet diameter, while sufficiently high ozone concentrations led to hot-flame transition after initiation.
findings.safety_implication: Ozone contamination and operating conditions can change whether a droplet sustains cool combustion or transitions to a hot flame, so these conditions matter when assessing ignition hazards around these fuels.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere controls and operating procedures involving ozone and pressure should account for their modeled influence on cool-to-hot flame transitions.
findings.source_quote: Comprehensive parametric computations show that the regime of the cool flame burning mode and the transition from cool to hot flames are sensitive to the changes of O3 loading, pressure, diluent variation, the strength of initiation source, and the influence of fuel vapor pressure at the ambient condition.

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter sized droplets; over a range of O3 concentrations in the ambient; over some range of O3 concentrations, operating pressure, and drop diameter
findings.quantity: sustained cool-flame burning and transition to hot flame
findings.statement: Computations predict that sub-millimeter n-heptane and n-decane droplets can sustain cool-flame burning across a range of ambient ozone concentrations, and that some ozone-concentration, pressure, and droplet-diameter conditions permit continuous self-sustaining cool flames without hot-flame transition.
findings.safety_implication: A cool flame can persist without becoming a hot flame, so absence of hot-flame transition does not by itself establish that combustion has ended.
findings.equipment_implication: Operational assessments should distinguish sustained cool-flame combustion from hot-flame transition when evaluating ozone and pressure conditions.
findings.source_quote: For both fuels and over a range of O3 concentrations in the ambient, sustained cool flame burning can be directly produced, even for sub-millimeter sized droplets. Over some range of O3 concentrations, operating pressure, and drop diameter, a self-sustaining, continuous cool flame burn can be produced without incurring a hot flame transition.

findings.conditions_text: sufficiently high O3 concentrations
findings.quantity: transition from cool flame to hot flame
findings.statement: The computations predict that sufficiently high ozone concentrations cause combustion initiation in n-heptane and n-decane droplets to be followed by a hot-flame transition.
findings.safety_implication: High ozone conditions may turn initiated droplet combustion into a hot flame, which should be considered when evaluating ignition hazards in ozone-containing environments.
findings.equipment_implication: Ozone-control limits and operating procedures should account for the predicted hot-flame transition at sufficiently high ozone concentrations.
findings.source_quote: For sufficiently high O3 concentrations, combustion initiation is always followed by a hot flame transition.

findings.conditions_text: in the air at atmospheric pressure
findings.quantity: droplet diameter associated with transition to cool-flame diffusive burning
findings.statement: In ISS experiments at atmospheric pressure, n-heptane droplets larger than approximately 4 mm initially undergo hot-flame radiative behavior that transitions to cool-flame diffusive burning; smaller n-heptane droplets exhibit only hot-flame burning, followed by diffusive extinction or complete liquid consumption.
findings.source_quote: For example, in experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS), large n-heptane (n-C7H16) droplets (Do > ~ 4 mm) ignited in the air at atmospheric pressure the hot flame phenomena occurring initially radiatively transitions to a cool flame diffusive burning mode [2]. For smaller n-heptane droplets that do not have an overwhelming radiative loss from the flame, only hot flame burning is observed, leading to diffusive extinction or complete liquid phase consumption.

findings.statement: For sub-millimeter n-heptane droplets, ozone-stimulated oxidation of initially present fuel vapor and initiation energy help establish sustained cool-flame burning, but heat release from that vapor can limit or prevent it.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition controls for low-flash-point fuels should account for fuel vapor already present near the droplet, since it can alter whether cool-flame burning is sustained.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for both initiation energy and the availability of fuel vapor when assessing cool-flame establishment.
findings.source_quote: In summary, the combined effects of initiation energy, and ozone-stimulated chemical heat release from initially present fuel vapor oxidation play key roles in establishing a sustained cool flame droplet burning behaviors for sub-millimeter sized low flash point fuels such as n-C7H16.

findings.statement: Experiments with large n-decane droplets in the ISS showed that when ambient temperature is below the fuel's flash point, ignition behavior depends more strongly on the applied thermal initiation energy; changing its deposition rate led to either hot-flame radiative extinction followed by prolonged cool-flame burning or direct cool-flame establishment.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition-energy delivery can change whether a droplet transitions through a hot flame or establishes a cool flame directly, which matters when evaluating ignition and flame-extinction behavior in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures and tests should account for the rate of thermal energy deposition when assessing cool-flame outcomes for fuels below their flash point.
findings.source_quote: Recent experiments with large diameter n-decane (n-C10H22) droplets on board the ISS demonstrated that for fuels and conditions where ambient temperatures are below the flash point, the overall ignition characteristics are significantly more dependent on the thermal initiation energy that is applied.

findings.quantity: droplet surface temperature at establishment of steady cool-flame combustion
findings.statement: In simulations of n-decane droplets, an initial cool-flame attempt consumed fuel without establishing steady combustion while fuel-vapor supply was insufficient; oscillatory cool flames followed, and steady cool-flame combustion became possible when the droplet surface approached ~ 400 K and evaporation increased.
findings.safety_implication: A transient flame or ignition event may not indicate sustained burning when vapor supply is limited, while subsequent droplet heating can enable steady combustion.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition assessments should distinguish transient cool-flame activity from sustained combustion as the droplet heats and vapor production changes.
findings.source_quote: Therefore, oscillatory cool flames are triggered (cf. Figure 6.6 (a), 7 (f) and 8 (d)) similar to those observed for large diameter droplets [4, 33]. By the time the second dumped cool flame reappears, liquid phase droplet surface temperature approaches ~ 400 K at which enhanced fuel evaporation is established which is sufficient to establish a steady cool flame combustion (cf. Figure 6.6 (a) and 7 (e)).

findings.statement: For isolated n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets, the initiation-energy requirements differ: partially premixed vapor combustion helps sustain low-flashpoint fuel burning as it transitions to diffusion burning, while high-flashpoint n-C10H22 liquid must first be heated above its flash temperature and the energy must also sustain that transition.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition strategies for liquid fuels should account for fuel flashpoint and vaporization because the energy needed to initiate and sustain burning differs between fuels.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for fuel-specific flashpoint and vaporization behavior.
findings.source_quote: The required initiation energy for igniting low and high flashpoint (relative to ambient temperature) fuel droplets differ as a result of combustion of partially premixed flammable vapor present in the low flashpoint case.

findings.conditions_text: Without ozone present
findings.statement: Without ozone, n-C7H16, the low-flashpoint fuel case, is difficult to keep from transitioning to hot-flame conditions because of the vapor temperature needed for ignition and the rate and duration of droplet vaporization.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition of low-flashpoint liquid fuels without ozone may produce hot flames rather than a controlled cool-flame state.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for the difficulty of avoiding hot-flame conditions in the low-flashpoint case without ozone.
findings.source_quote: Without ozone present, the fuel/vapor temperature required to initiate the burning of the low flash point fuel and the rate and duration of vaporization of the droplet makes it difficult to avoid the transition to hot flame conditions.

findings.statement: Without ozone, limited vaporization in the high-flashpoint fuel case allows the initiation energy's rate and duration to be controlled to achieve cool-flame burning without hot-flame conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel volatility and control of ignition energy can affect whether ignition produces cool-flame or hot-flame burning.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for fuel vaporization and control the rate and duration of initiation energy.
findings.source_quote: Without ozone present, and with the limited vaporization typical of high flash point fuels, the initiation energy can be controlled in terms of rate and duration to achieve cool flame burning without incurring hot flame conditions.

findings.conditions_text: O3 seeded into the surrounding air
findings.quantity: initiation temperature and energy release rate
findings.statement: For n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets, ozone seeding reduces the temperature, and therefore the initiation energy, required to initiate gas-phase reactions; the ozone amount affects the rate of energy release at and after reaction initiation.
findings.safety_implication: Ozone concentration can alter ignition requirements and subsequent energy release, so it is a relevant atmospheric condition when assessing ignition behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere assessments should account for ozone concentration because it affects both initiation requirements and energy release after ignition.
findings.source_quote: The seeding of O3 into the surrounding air offers an ability to reduce the temperature (and therefore initiation energy required) to initiate gas phase reactions of the flammable vapor/air mixtures. The amount of O3 seeding affects the rate of energy release occurring at and subsequent to reaction initiation.

findings.safety_implication: Higher pressure can make hot ignition possible at a lower ozone threshold, so ignition risk assessments should consider pressure and ozone together.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere hazard assessments should account for the interaction of pressure and ozone concentration when evaluating ignition regimes.
findings.source_quote: At elevated pressure (here, 25 atm), the requirement for threshold maximum O3 concentration that drives the system to hot ignition decreases significantly due to the pressure dependence of reactions forming HO2 and especially the H2O2 (+M) = OH + OH (+M).

findings.statement: In simulations of 0.5 mm n-heptane droplets at 1 atm and 298 K with 5% ozone seeding, reducing ambient oxygen below the approximately 13% limiting oxygen index still allowed a quasi-steady cool flame to establish, after an induction time of about 0.12 s; its predicted temperature was about 710 K.

findings.quantity: droplet diameter regression agreement with measurements
findings.statement: The detailed and reduced kinetic models predicted n-Butanol droplet-diameter regressions that agreed well with measurements up to approximately 50% of burn-time; after that, deviations grew, with the reduced model deviating more than the detailed model.
findings.source_quote: Up to approximately 50% of the burn, predictions from the model are almost identical and are in very good agreement with the measured data. However, beyond 50% of the burn-time slight deviation between the predictions and measurements start to exist. The discrepancy with the measurements increases when the reduced kinetic model is employed compared to the detailed kinetic model, as expected since reduced kinetic models removed possibly finer kinetic aspects during the process of reduction.

findings.quantity: model accuracy for burning rates and flame stand-off ratios
findings.statement: For butanol-isomer droplet combustion, the Sarathy et al. kinetic-model predictions overestimated burning rates and flame stand-off ratios for all isomers except n-butanol, while Merchant et al.-based predictions agreed better with experiment, with larger discrepancies for tert-butanol.
findings.source_quote: DNM predictions based on the kinetic model of Sarathy et al. over-predict the droplet burning rates and FSRs of all the isomers except n -butanol. Predictions using a kinetic model based on the  work of Merchant et al. agree much better with the experimental data, though relatively higher discrepancies are evident for tert-butanol simulation results.

findings.conditions_text: For an individual isomer, respective simulations are performed under the same level of initial ignition energy. Ambient condition for simulation: P = 1 atm, T = 298 K.
findings.quantity: predicted gas-temperature rise and maximum gas temperature
findings.statement: For sec-, iso-, and tert-butanol droplet simulations at the same initial ignition energy, the LLNL model predicted earlier temperature rises than the MIT model, while both predicted nearly the same maximum gas temperature after ignition except during flame-out.
findings.source_quote: It is perceptible from the figure that the LLNL model ignition chemistry for each of the isomers is more sensitive than its counterpart model. Therefore, the rise in temperature for LLNL model is consistently earlier than that of MIT model. Surprisingly, immediately after the ignition transient, both the model approaches to the same maximum temperature throughout the lifetime of the burning droplet (i.e., at least till LLNL model predicted lifetime), both profiles remain almost the same except the flame-out phase.

findings.conditions_text: n-decane droplets (Do ~ 4 mm); controlling the hot wire initiation energy– current amplitude and duration
findings.statement: For approximately 4 mm n-decane droplets, controlling hot-wire initiation energy through current amplitude and duration can produce either direct cool-flame burning or hot-flame burning; numerical analyses attribute this control to modulation of flammable fuel-air mixture formation near the droplet surface.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures for n-decane droplets can use hot-wire current amplitude and duration to select between direct cool-flame and hot-flame burning modes.
findings.source_quote: However, in more recent ISS experiments using n-decane (n-C10H22) droplets (Do ~ 4 mm) [5], cool flame behavior was able to be achieved directly by controlling the hot wire initiation energy– current amplitude and duration. Numerical analyses reveal that as a result of the high flashpoint of n-decane (319.3 K [8]), modulation of the initiation energy can be utilized to control the formation rate of partially premixed flammable fuel/air mixtures near the drop surface, and hence, control the heat release associated with vapor phase reaction.

findings.conditions_text: two initial droplet diameters (Do = 0.1 and 0.5 mm) and two ambient air pressures (1 and 30 atm) seeded with different levels of O3
findings.statement: For sub-millimeter n-heptane and n-decane droplets, the study computationally evaluates whether adding ozone can directly induce cool-flame burning at initial diameters of 0.1 and 0.5 mm and ambient pressures of 1 and 30 atm; this passage reports the study objective and conditions, not the outcomes.
findings.source_quote: The primary objective of this study is to computationally evaluate the potential of O3 addition to directly induce cool flame burning for sub-millimeter sized low and high flash point fuels, i.e. for n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets, respectively. Below, we investigate two initial droplet diameters (Do = 0.1 and 0.5 mm) and two ambient air pressures (1 and 30 atm) seeded with different levels of O3.

findings.statement: For a 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet at 1 atm with 3% O3, simulations predicted that the prescribed thermal ignition source initiated and stabilized the cool flame faster than the hot-ambient ignition approach.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition method can affect observed ignition timing, so comparisons of ignition behavior should control or document the method used.
findings.equipment_implication: Combustion-test procedures should specify the ignition-energy deposition method when comparing ignition times.
findings.source_quote: Therefore, for the remainder of this article, all results and discussions are based on the prescribed thermal ignition source.

findings.conditions_text: 0.5 mm droplet at 1 atm (3% O3, producing cool flame) and 25 atm (0.5% O3)
findings.statement: For 0.5 mm n-heptane droplets, numerical simulations indicate that raising pressure from 1 atm to 25 atm shifts burning toward hot ignition, with elevated pressure making the H2O2 decomposition pathway to OH more important.
findings.source_quote: At atmospheric pressure, the relative importance of H2O2 in transitioning the gas phase reactive mixture to hot ignition via H2O2 (+M) = OH + OH (+M) is much less pronounced than the elevated pressure scenario where the O3 loading is purposely made small. At higher pressure, the drastic consumption of H2O2 and the evolution of gas phase temperature and OH radicals (cf. subplots in bottom row) manifest the impact of pressure in shifting the system to hot ignition.
